title: Predictive low rank matrix learning under partial observations: Mixed-projection ADMM
contribution: Introduces a matrix-completion problem in which the reconstruction must also linearly predict fully observed side information (Problem (1)). The paper shows (1) is equivalent to a robust problem, reformulates it exactly with projection matrices, gives an SDP relaxation that is never solved, and builds an ADMM whose four blocks have closed forms, with an a posteriori stationarity theorem. At small rank the ADMM is level with Fast-Impute-Side on objective and cuts reconstruction error by about 40%; it loses for k > 10; on Netflix data it beats Fast-Impute out of sample in far less time. No gaps or certificates are reported (arXiv v3).
problem_entry: ML, with IO/CP formulation devices and an RO reading. Matrix completion with fully observed side information assumed linear in the true matrix (abstract, p. 1). Entry via an assumption of prior work, which fixes a structural parametrization of the matrix (p. 2); here the side information is instead the label of a regression whose features are the unobserved matrix, after Bach and Jordan 2005 (p. 2). Problem (1) combines a rank constraint, a nuclear norm and a least-squares side-information term (p. 2) and is claimed not previously studied (p. 3). No owner, decision or why-now argument (the skill's Method 2 term) (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: A projection matrix P models the column space of X, so the least-squares projection term becomes lambda Tr(Y^T(I-P)Y) under (I-P)X = 0 and tr P <= k (pp. 11-12). X is factored as UV^T, with the nuclear norm replaced by (gamma/2)(||U||^2+||V||^2), and P is stored as MM^T (pp. 13, 23). A copy Z = U and an indicator of P_k make every ADMM block closed-form: row-wise ridge solves for U and V, a truncated SVD for P computed without forming the n x n matrix, Woodbury for Z (pp. 16-23). The shift from the group's earlier papers: from SDP relaxations and certified small instances to scalable feasible solutions (pp. 6-7).
assumptions: Nonconvex, nonsmooth objective (Prop. 2, p. 9); A low rank and Y = A alpha + N (p. 3). lambda and gamma may take a default value or be cross-validated (p. 3), but the values used in Section 6 are not stated, nor is the tolerance epsilon (pp. 27-29). The algorithm solves relaxation (8), which can be strictly looser in pathological cases (p. 14). The SDP relaxation needs a bound M taken from the objective value of X = 0 (pp. 14-15). Theorem 13 assumes bounded dual iterates with summable steps and an eigenvector condition checkable only at termination (pp. 24, 27). The synthetic data are generated from the model's own linear assumption (p. 29) [inferred: a well-specified regime]. Real data: Netflix Prize with six TMDB features (pp. 39-40).
proof_devices: Regularization as robustness through nuclear/spectral norm duality, with worst case gamma UV^T (Prop. 1, pp. 8-9)
Nonconvexity shown by restricting f to a line in a 2-D instance with two chord violations (Prop. 2, pp. 9-10); my recomputation confirms the values; typo fX(0.5) for fX(-0.5)
Evaluation through an SVD, cutting the cost to O(kn(m+d)) (Prop. 3, pp. 10-11)
Exactness of the reformulation by uniqueness of the orthogonal projection (Prop. 4, pp. 12-13), and of the factorized form via the Mazumder-Hastie-Tibshirani identity (Props. 5-6, pp. 13-14)
SDP relaxation from the matrix perspective and the convex hull of P_k, valid by the generalized Schur complement; eigenvector disjunctions named for tightening (Prop. 7, pp. 14-16)

Closed-form ADMM blocks with complexity counts: row-separable ridge solves (Props. 8-9, pp. 17-19); a Ky Fan-type P-step with a truncated SVD of F1 F2^T computed without forming it (Prop. 10, pp. 20-22); a Woodbury Z-step (Prop. 11, pp. 22-23); per-iteration complexity (Prop. 12, p. 24)

A posteriori convergence (Theorem 13, pp. 24-27): strong convexity gives sufficient decrease; the Lagrangian is bounded below by completing squares; limit points satisfy KKT under an eigenvector condition, which is turned into a dual residual (p. 27). My check: a constant slip (-rho instead of -1/rho) and a sign slip in (24) on p. 25, harmless under the assumptions
experiments: Julia 1.7.3, rho = 10, T = 20, 24 threads, Xeon Platinum 8260 (pp. 27-28). Baselines: Fast-Impute and Fast-Impute-Side (the group's own JMLR 2020 code); Soft-Impute and Iterative-SVD (fancyimpute 0.7.0); a self-implemented ScaledGD at default hyperparameters, whose relative errors are far above 1 (pp. 28-31, 49). Synthetic sweeps of n, m, d and k, 20 trials each (pp. 29-39): reconstruction error 23-77% below the best alternative; objective level with Fast-Impute-Side, which wins by orders of magnitude at k > 10 (pp. 31-38, 51). Netflix + TMDB with 20% holdouts: 67% lower out-of-sample error and 97% less time than Fast-Impute where it finished; the others timed out at 20 h (pp. 40-42). Over-fitting as k grows is admitted (p. 42). My recomputation from Tables A1-A15: error 42.5% lower and best in 23 of 26 small-rank configurations; on objective Fast-Impute-Side is lower in 15 of 26, and the mean difference ranges from -2.7% to +3.2% against the claimed 2.3%; Netflix 68.0% and 97.1%. Not reported: lambda, gamma, epsilon; any gap or solve of the SDP; any n = m = 10,000 run (p. 48); tests.
positioning: One representative per MC family serves as a baseline (pp. 4-6), and rivals are restated respectfully (p. 5). Side-information approaches impose fixed structure; Bach and Jordan 2005 is the precedent (p. 2). The paper is the scale branch of the group's mixed-projection programme (refs [17, 38, 40, 41], pp. 6-7) and reuses its robustness-regularization dictionary (ref [49], p. 8). The convergence frame comes from the nonconvex ADMM literature (pp. 7, 24, 27). Ten of the 61 references are the group's own (pp. 55-59).
writing: The abstract leads with five headline numbers (p. 1), repeated in Section 1.1 with a claim about k > 15 (p. 3). Proposition-proof body with complexity paragraphs (pp. 7-24); numbered findings per sweep, with losses in the body (pp. 30-44). Gaps between headline and body: Fast-Impute-Side is better and faster than Algorithm 1 at every k >= 15 (p. 51), against the p. 3 sentence; no n = m = 10,000 run (p. 48); the 'strong' relaxation is untested (pp. 1, 45). Two Declarations blocks give different statements of who designed the algorithm (pp. 46, 54). Small slips (pp. 8, 10, 24).
limits_future: Contribution: a problem, formulation theory, an algorithm with complexity counts and an a posteriori theorem, open code, and a large real-data test (pp. 3, 44-45). Limits stated: the k > 10 regime (pp. 43-44), over-fitting as the rank grows (p. 42), the a posteriori nature of Theorem 13 (p. 27), the possibly looser relaxation (8) (p. 14). Future: PSD and linear constraints; test the strength of (9) and use it to certify global optimality (p. 45). Unstated [inferred]: misspecified side information, sensitivity to lambda and gamma, distance of the output from the bound.

method_links.note: A problem owned by ML is rewritten exactly in the mixed-projection class, with a dual (RO) reading and an SDP relaxation (Props. 1, 4-7). But no off-the-shelf solver handles the class: a bespoke ADMM runs on relaxation (8), and the SDP is never solved. The method's distinguishing move (SKILL.md Method 1: the model, not the algorithm, is redesigned so existing solvers apply) is inverted. The boundary is printed: looseness of (8) (p. 14), the a posteriori theorem (p. 27), losses at k > 10 (pp. 43-44).

Present: a truncated-SVD warm start (pp. 23-24); runtime settings stated, though lambda, gamma and epsilon are missing (pp. 27-28); duels on synthetic data with known truth and on Netflix holdouts against public code, including the group's own Fast-Impute (pp. 28, 40-42); losses printed (pp. 38, 43-44). Missing: no exact solve, certificate or gap; certification is deferred (p. 45), so only 'high quality feasible solutions' are claimed (p. 1). Workflow D / T6 echo: the abstract claims '2.3% lower objective', though Fast-Impute-Side is lower in 15 of 26 small-rank configurations (my recomputation, pp. 47-51), and Tables A12-A14 contradict the k > 15 sentence of p. 3 (p. 51). Not counted: Heuristic 1 evidence (Prop. 1 reuses card S085's dictionary, pp. 8-9); Heuristic 9 partly (headline numbers but no opening about the community's belief, p. 1); Taste mark 4 and Methods 2, 3 and 5 not engaged.

A thesis lineage carries the programme (step 3). Ten self-references tie the paper to the mixed-projection line (Cory-Wright, Pauphilet, Lo; refs [17, 38, 40, 41]) and to Johnson's earlier papers with Bertsimas (refs [40, 55]). The contribution statements show the student implementing, running the experiments and drafting (pp. 46, 54). Course, book and company steps are not visible.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: closed-form-block ADMM on an exact mixed-projection reformulation (scale branch, certification deferred)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The exact reformulation and the SDP relaxation stay on paper (Props. 4-7). The experiments run a splitting whose four blocks are closed-form (Props. 8-11). The paper positions itself explicitly against the group's relaxation and certification papers (pp. 6-7) and leaves certification to future work (p. 45).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: a posteriori stationarity condition turned into a plotted dual residual
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Theorem 13's eigenvector condition can be checked only at termination. The authors rewrite it as (I - P1)P2 = 0, call P2 - P1P2 a dual residual, and plot it with the primal residuals over 500 iterations (pp. 24, 27-28).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: regularize to convexify the value function, then price the regularizer (card S250 candidate; first half only)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The Frobenius terms that come from gamma||X||_* make the U- and V-blocks strongly convex and their inverses well defined; with gamma = 0 the V-step matrix can be singular (p. 19). gamma is never priced, and its value is not reported (pp. 27-29).

transferable: Replace a projection term built from a pseudo-inverse, X(X^T X)^+ X^T, by a projection-matrix variable P with (I - P)X = 0 and tr P <= k, stored as P = MM^T so it costs n x k memory (pp. 11-13, 23)

Split with a copy Z = U and an indicator of the nonconvex set so that every ADMM block is closed-form: row-wise k x k ridge solves, a truncated SVD for the projection block, Woodbury for the coupling block (pp. 16-23)
Compute the truncated SVD of C = F1 F2^T without forming C, through a custom matrix-vector product via the factors, O(n(d + k)) per product (pp. 21-22)
Bound the spectral norm of any optimal solution by the trivial solution's objective value divided by gamma, to get the big-M-like constant a perspective relaxation needs (pp. 14-15)
For a nonconvex ADMM, prove the a posteriori KKT result under bounded, summable dual steps, then turn its checkable condition into a dual residual plotted next to the primal residuals (pp. 24-28)
Prove that an objective is neither convex nor concave by restricting it to a line in a 2-D instance and exhibiting one chord violation of each kind (pp. 9-10)
Time each algorithm block in every sweep and check the empirical scaling against that block's complexity count (Figs. 4, 7, 10, 13; pp. 32-44)
coauthors: Nicholas A. G. Johnson (Operations Research Center, MIT; corresponding author; equal contribution)

quotes.text: In this work, we leverage the mixed-projection framework to scalably obtain high quality solutions to large problem instances.
Additionally, future work could empirically investigate the strength of the semidefinite relaxation (9) and could explore how to leverage this lower bound to certify globally optimal solutions.

title: Wfdronebench: A benchmark for sensor placement and drone routing for wildfire detection
contribution: A student-led open benchmark (a library, 7,746 semi-synthetic fire scenarios on 49 layouts, five strategies) that couples ML wildfire risk maps to MILP/LP sensor placement and rolling-horizon drone routing, and scores them by simulated detection. On a 474-scenario subset, risk-aware routing pays only with an accurate (oracle) map, uniform coverage is safer with the operational map, and the risk map, not routing, is named the bottleneck. No gaps, literature baselines or tests are reported (arXiv v3).
problem_entry: AP + IO + DA. Wildfire damages and the limits of sensors and satellites (p. 2); most drone studies assume predefined flight paths, and active routing for early detection is 'largely unaddressed' (p. 2). Stated goal: minimize the expected detection delay over the ignition distribution by placing sensors and stations and routing drones under a burn-risk field from simulation or ML (p. 3). Form of contribution: a benchmark for the ML and OR communities (pp. 2-4). No agency or owner is engaged (p. 9).
key_idea: Score predictive risk maps and deployment policies jointly by simulated detection (p. 4). Placement: GaussianCov max coverage, with charging-station coverage from a Brownian-motion visit kernel (pp. 6-7, 15). Routing: a rolling-horizon, risk-weighted maximum unique coverage MILP (MaxCov), with a uniform-risk ablation (UniCov) and random walks as baselines (pp. 7-8, 16-17). A zone decomposition for scale (pp. 6, 13-14). The optimized objective is coverage, not the stated expected detection delay (pp. 3, 10).
assumptions: Grid and discrete time; a fire is detected when it enters a sensing radius (p. 3). Binary placement, flight, charging and coverage variables; battery recursion; one-cell moves; a communication radius (pp. 3-5, Table 1). Risk is lowered where drones fly (p. 5). Sim2Real-Fire spread matched to FPA FOD ignitions: 7,746 scenarios on 49 layouts, tagged by size, speed and match, with a random 1-12 h delay (p. 5). Test on 12 layouts and 474 scenarios with at least 80% match (p. 8). Risk maps: the USDA BP map (30 m in the text vs a 270-m product in the references, pp. 7, 11, 20) and an oracle map averaged from the simulations (p. 7) [inferred: possibly in-sample]. 8 sensors, 2 drones, 2 stations (p. 8). Drone parameters differ from the cited Mugin EV350 specification (p. 7 vs Table 6, p. 14). Admitted: no communication failures, terrain or execution uncertainty; full observability; no weather effects (p. 9).
proof_devices: n/a for proofs or bounds; formulation devices only
Max-coverage placement with indirect fractional coverage, solved as an LP (App. E.1, p. 15)
Brownian-motion visit kernel for charging-station coverage, computed by iterative 3x3 convolutions capped at 1 (pp. 6-7, 15)
Routing MILP (2a)-(2n): fly-or-charge, capacity, one-cell motion, battery recursion, a terminal 'no-suicide' constraint, monotone coverage (App. E.2, pp. 16-17)
Rolling horizon: solve over H = 10, execute T_reev = 5, update the risk, re-solve (pp. 16-17; Table 6, p. 14)
Greedy decomposition into zones of charging stations within battery range (Algorithm 1, pp. 13-14)
Optional dispersion reward, linearized with big-M constraints (p. 17)
experiments: Julia 1.11.3, JuMP 1.26.0, Gurobi 12.0.3; Xeon Platinum 8260 cluster, 32 CPUs and 125 GB per job (p. 8); under 30 s of computation per hour of operation (p. 8). Tables 2-3 (p. 9): with the BP map, UniCov detects as much as MaxCov or more (93% vs 91%; 97% vs 96%) and 100% of fast fires, while MaxCov detects 73% in Fast Big. With the oracle map, MaxCov is faster overall (2.49 vs 3.74 h with random sensors; 3.20 vs 3.41 h with GaussianCov) at similar rates, but faster in only 4 of the 8 size-speed cells; with GaussianCov the oracle map leaves MaxCov unchanged (3.16 h and 96% vs 3.20 h and 95%). GaussianCov beats Random in 20 of 30 rate cells (equal in 7, lower in 3). Drones make 71.5-100% of detections (p. 19). Baselines are the authors' own ablations and random strategies; no literature method is run (p. 3). SDs are printed but no tests, although the text says 'significantly' (pp. 1, 9); my rough unpaired check: the 0.21 h gap is about 0.7 SE, the 1.25 h gap about 4 SE. Mean detection time is defined over detected fires (p. 14) but over all scenarios on p. 5. 474 of 7,746 scenarios tested (p. 8). Code and data released (p. 10).
positioning: Related work is characterized by the operational constraint each line omits: MILP watchtower/balloon placement with single missions and no recharging (De la Fuente et al. 2024); probabilistic path planning by logistic regression and DP; makespan models; Gaussian-mixture partitioning; PSO; UAV-routing surveys (p. 3). None is run as a baseline. The paper's own placement extends Church and ReVelle 1974 (p. 6). Datasets: Sim2Real-Fire, FPA FOD, USDA BP (pp. 5, 7). No Bertsimas work is cited; one coauthor self-citation (Trisovic, ref [16], p. 11).
writing: Abstract: threat, monitoring limits, drones, library, contents, three findings, two open challenges, release (p. 1). Four bold contributions (pp. 2-3); dollar-damage motivation (p. 2); findings as an ordinal list (pp. 8-9). Inference is hedged ('suggests', p. 9), but 'significantly' appears without tests (pp. 1, 9). Call for ML work on risk maps (pp. 1, 10). Benchmark apparatus: availability statements, licence table, README pointer (pp. 10, 20) [inferred: written for a datasets-and-benchmarks venue]. Slips: 'six' strategies counted as two plus three (p. 3); Brownian described as both risk-proportional and risk-ignoring (p. 7); UniCov described two ways (pp. 7-8); a number from the BP table used for the accurate-map case (pp. 8-9); 30 m vs 270 m (pp. 7, 11, 20); mixed table captions and 0.000 routing times (p. 19); Gurobi 8.1.1 manual vs version 12.0.3 (pp. 8, 11).
limits_future: An infrastructure contribution plus the finding that accurate dynamic burn-probability maps, not routing, are the bottleneck (p. 9). Limits stated specifically: communication, terrain and execution uncertainty abstracted away; full observability; no weather effects, which the hourly rolling horizon is argued to absorb (p. 9). Future: RL, weather-conditioned dynamic maps, routing that minimizes expected detection time, heterogeneous fleets, real-time coupling of predictions and decisions, historical propagation data, policy and hardware analyses. Open challenges: small fires and risk-map prediction (p. 10). Unstated [inferred]: MILP gaps, literature baselines, the 7,272 untested scenarios, tests, whether the oracle map is out of sample.

method_links.note: Decisions, not predictions, are scored (steps 4-5): risk maps are judged by their impact on detection with routing fixed (p. 4), and the result is which policy suits which map quality (pp. 8-9). But there is no owner, data holder or current rule: the baselines are random and uniform ablations; the predefined flight paths most studies assume (p. 2) are not benchmarked; agencies are a future audience (p. 9); there is no field test (step 6).

Placement and routing are written as LP/MILP coverage models solved by Gurobi through JuMP, kept tractable by a rolling horizon and a zone decomposition, with times measured at the operating cadence (under 30 s per hour of operation, p. 8). Only the class-keeping and measured-time part of the method; no dual reading or printed boundary.

The exact MILP is the engine, but no time limit, gap or certificate is reported. The opponents are uninformed ablations, not the incumbent heuristics reviewed on p. 3. The headline 'significantly outperforms' (pp. 1, 9) is untested and holds for the Overall column only (Table 3, p. 9): Tension T6. Not counted: Heuristic 6 evidence (a data asset is built and prediction is split from selection, pp. 4-5, 10); Taste mark 1 consistent (agencies named as future users, p. 9); Methods 2, 3 and 6 not engaged.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: decision-coupled benchmark: score predictive models by the decisions they induce, in one open library for ML and OR
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: ML researchers test risk maps by detection with routing fixed, and OR researchers test routing on a shared map (p. 4); scenarios, metrics, code and data are released (pp. 5-6, 10).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: perfect-information input as an upper bound that separates prediction error from policy error
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: An oracle dynamic map averaged from the simulations is run beside the operational BP map; the change of best routing policy between Tables 2 and 3 is read as the value of better risk prediction (pp. 7-9).

transferable: Model the indirect coverage of a facility that serves mobile agents by the visit probability of a random walk from the facility, computed by repeated 3x3 convolutions and capped at 1, inside a max-coverage location model (pp. 6-7, 15)
In rolling-horizon routing with energy limits, add a terminal 'no-suicide' constraint (end-of-horizon battery >= distance to the nearest station) so that truncated plans stay recoverable (p. 16)
Ablate an optimization policy by feeding it a uniform input (a uniform risk map) to isolate the value of the input information (p. 8)
Run the operational predictor beside an oracle input built from the simulator to bound what better prediction could buy, and report both tables side by side (pp. 7-9)
Add a random delay (1-12 h) to ignition times so that policies cannot exploit a fixed onset time (p. 5)
Tag benchmark scenarios by difficulty attributes (size, spread rate, historical and seasonal match) and report results per category (pp. 5, 9)
coauthors: Romain Puech (ORC, MIT; first author), Joseph Ye (Sloan, MIT; listed in v3, absent from the work list), Danique de Moor (Sloan, MIT), Ana Trišović (CSAIL, MIT); Bertsimas last

quotes.text: ML researchers can benchmark risk models via their impact on detection with fixed routing and OR experts can compare routing strategies on a shared risk map.
We identify that the bottleneck for drone-based wildfire detection systems lies in developing accurate, temporally dynamic burn probability maps rather than routing optimization alone
